item: Write down the scope boundary: which business units, networks and locations are in, and agree it with the assessor before starting.
Include every end-user device that can reach organisational data or services. A scope that leaves out user devices is not acceptable.
Keep an up-to-date inventory of in-scope devices (servers, user devices, firewalls, routers) showing owner, operating system and support status.
List every cloud service that holds or processes organisational data, who is responsible for each control (you or the provider), and keep all of them in scope.
Decide whether personal devices (BYOD) may access organisational data. Those that do are in scope; keep a list or block them.
Cover home and remote working: devices used at home are in scope, and a router supplied by the organisation is in scope.
If anything is excluded, justify the exclusion, explain how it is separated from the rest, and list every legal entity that is in scope.
Bring accounts used by suppliers, contractors and managed service providers into scope, and any organisation-owned device lent to a third party.
Protect every in-scope device with a correctly configured firewall: a boundary firewall, or a firewall on the device itself.
Change the default administrator password on firewalls and routers to a strong, unique one, or switch remote administration off.
Do not expose firewall administration pages to the internet unless there is a documented business need and either MFA or an allow list of trusted addresses is in place.
Block unauthenticated inbound connections by default and only open what is needed.
Have each inbound rule approved and documented by an authorised person, with the business reason recorded.
Remove or disable inbound rules as soon as they are no longer needed.
Run a software firewall on devices that are used on untrusted networks such as home or public Wi-Fi.
For cloud services, use the provider's network and data flow controls (for example access rules and allow lists) where a firewall cannot be used.
Regularly remove or disable accounts that are not needed, including guest, default and unused administrator accounts.
Change default or easily guessed passwords on every device and application.
Remove or disable software, utilities and network services that are not needed.
Turn off auto-run features that start files without the user choosing to.
Make sure users are authenticated before they can reach organisational data or services.
Lock devices: require a password, PIN or biometric to unlock, and limit repeated guessing (for example no more than 10 attempts, or throttling).
Make sure all in-scope software is licensed and still supported by its vendor.
Remove software that has gone out of support, or take the device out of scope using a separated network sub-set that has no internet access.
Turn on automatic updates wherever the product offers them.
Install operating system and firmware updates within 14 days of release when they fix vulnerabilities rated critical or high, scored 7 or more on CVSS v3, or have no severity given.
Install application updates, including browser extensions and plug-ins, within 14 days of release under the same severity rules.
If an update bundles several fixes and any one is critical or high, install the whole bundle within 14 days.
Practical measure: be able to show which in-scope devices are missing critical or high updates older than 14 days, including devices that are offline.
Have a process to request, approve and create user accounts.
Give each person unique credentials before they can use applications or devices; avoid shared accounts.
Remove or disable accounts when they are no longer needed, for example when someone leaves or after a set period of inactivity.
Turn on MFA for every cloud service that offers it, whether the option is free, bundled or paid.
Require MFA on administrator accounts and on any account that can be reached from the internet.
Use separate administrator accounts for administration only, never for email, web browsing or everyday work.
Take away special privileges when they are no longer needed, for example after a change of role.
Where passwords are used, protect against guessing with MFA, throttling (no more than 10 guesses in 5 minutes) or lockout after no more than 10 failures.
Apply a password quality control: MFA, or at least 12 characters, or at least 8 characters with common passwords blocked.
Help people choose unique passwords, for example by providing a password manager and guidance on long passphrases, and do not force routine expiry.
Have a process to change passwords promptly when a compromise is known or suspected.
Apply the same account controls to third-party accounts such as support and managed service provider logins.
Have a malware protection method active on every in-scope device.
If using anti-malware software, keep it updated, make sure it stops malware running, and make it block known malicious websites.
If using application allow listing, only approved, validly signed applications may run, the approved list is kept current, and users cannot install unsigned ones.
Practical measure: check regularly that protection is present and current on every device, including new builds and laptops that are rarely online.
